actions.justification: Mandatory first step: assess hemodynamic stability to determine transfusion urgency and guide further management.
Mandatory: determine if active bleeding is present, which influences transfusion threshold and whether massive transfusion protocol is needed.
Mandatory: review prior transfusion history for alloantibodies, reactions, or special requirements that affect blood product selection.
Mandatory action: CBC is required to determine hemoglobin level and guide transfusion threshold decisions (restrictive vs liberal) per transfusion guidelines.
Mandatory action: Type and screen must be performed before any blood product administration to ensure compatibility and prevent transfusion reactions.

Optional but clinically indicated: Assessing symptoms of anemia (fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, dizziness) will help determine clinical urgency and guide the choice of restrictive vs liberal transfusion threshold alongside CBC results.

Patient is hemodynamically stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%) with no active bleeding signs. Evidence-based guidelines support a restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb <7-8 g/dL) in stable patients, which reduces transfusion-related risks while maintaining adequate oxygenation.
Administer acetaminophen as pre-transfusion medication to reduce febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions, consistent with standard transfusion premedication protocols.
Administer diphenhydramine as pre-transfusion premedication to prevent allergic/urticarial transfusion reactions, especially relevant if patient has prior transfusion history being reviewed.
Ensuring reliable IV access is essential for ongoing blood product administration and emergency interventions in this transfusion patient.
Maintaining normothermia is critical during transfusion to prevent hypothermia-induced coagulopathy and reduce transfusion complications.
Given the transfusion context with completed restrictive threshold assessment, evaluating whether a liberal transfusion threshold (Hb 8) is appropriate based on patient symptoms and clinical status.
Patient is stable but ongoing monitoring every 15 minutes is essential to detect any hemodynamic changes, signs of transfusion reaction, or clinical deterioration while awaiting CBC results.
Coagulation studies are important to assess bleeding risk and guide potential transfusion decisions, especially relevant in a transfusion workup context.
Iron studies help identify the etiology of anemia (iron deficiency vs. other causes) and guide further management decisions beyond transfusion.
Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is indicated to evaluate for hemolytic transfusion reaction or autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is important to rule out in this transfusion patient context.
Reticulocyte count helps assess bone marrow response to anemia and differentiates hypoproliferative from hemolytic or blood loss etiologies — important secondary workup while CBC is pending.
Thromboelastography (TEG) provides real-time assessment of coagulation function and guides targeted blood product administration, complementing the coagulation monitoring already in progress.
Patient is 90 minutes in with labs still pending. Reassess hemodynamic status to determine if clinical condition has changed and to guide transfusion decisions once CBC results return.
CBC is pending; reassessing hemoglobin trend is essential to determine transfusion threshold applicability and guide next steps in management.
Ensure blood bank workup is complete (type and crossmatch, antibody screen results) so that compatible blood products are ready if transfusion becomes necessary based on pending CBC results.
CBC is pending; pre-emptively set conditional transfusion order for Hb < 7 g/dL per restrictive transfusion threshold guideline, consistent with the already-applied restrictive threshold assessment.

If there is ongoing or occult bleeding in this transfusion workup context, tranexamic acid reduces fibrinolysis and can reduce transfusion requirements. Appropriate to administer while awaiting full lab results.
Patient is being monitored for transfusion reactions; furosemide should be given if transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is identified during ongoing monitoring.
